title: The True Cost of Food

bodyParagraphs: For more than forty years the cost of food has been rising. It has now reached a point where a growing number of people believe that it is far too high, and that bringing it down will be one of the great challenges of the twenty first century. That cost, however, is not in immediate cash. In the West at least, most food is now far cheaper to buy in relative terms than it was in 1960. The cost is in the collateral damage of the very methods of food production that have made the food cheaper: in the pollution of water, the enervation of soil, the destruction of wildlife, the harm to animal welfare and the threat to human health caused by modern industrial agriculture.

First mechanisation, then mass use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, then monocultures, then battery rearing of livestock, and now genetic engineering — the onward march of intensive farming has seemed unstoppable in the last half-century, as the yields of produce have soared. But the damage it has caused has been colossal. In Britain, for example, many of our best-loved farmland birds, such as the skylark, the grey partridge, the lapwing and the corn bunting, have vanished from huge stretches of countryside, as have even more wild flowers and insects. This is a direct result of the way we have produced our food in the last four decades. Thousands of miles of hedgerows, thousands of ponds, have disappeared from the landscape. The faecal filth of salmon farming has driven wild salmon from many of the sea lochs and rivers of Scotland. Natural soil fertility is dropping in many areas because of continuous industrial fertiliser and pesticide use, while the growth of algae is increasing in lakes because of the fertiliser run-off.

Put it all together and it looks like a battlefield, but consumers rarely make the connection at the dinner table. That is mainly because the costs of all this damage are what economists refer to as externalities: they are outside the main transaction, which is for example producing and selling a field of wheat, and are borne directly by neither producers nor consumers. To many, the costs may not even appear to be financial at all, but merely aesthetic – a terrible shame, but nothing to do with money. And anyway they, as consumers of food, certainly aren’t paying for it, are they?

But the costs to society can actually be quantified and, when added up, can amount to staggering sums. A remarkable exercise in doing this has been carried out by one of the world’s leading thinkers on the future of agriculture, Professor Jules Pretty, Director of the Centre for Environment and Society at the University of Essex. Professor Pretty and his colleagues calculated the externalities of British agriculture for one particular year. They added up the costs of repairing the damage it caused, and came up with a total figure of £2,343m. This is equivalent to £208 for every hectare of arable land and permanent pasture, almost as much again as the total government and EU spend on British farming in that year. And according to Professor Pretty, it was a conservative estimate.

The costs included: £120m for removal of pesticides; £16m for removal of nitrates; £55m for removal of phosphates and soil; £23m for the removal of the bug cryptosporidium from drinking water by water companies; £125m for damage to wildlife habitats, hedgerows and dry stone walls; £1,113m from emissions of gases likely to contribute to climate change; £106m from soil erosion and organic carbon losses; £169m from food poisoning; and £607m from cattle disease. Professor Pretty draws a simple but memorable conclusion from all this: our food bills are actually threefold. We are paying for our supposedly cheaper food in three separate ways: once over the counter, secondly through our taxes, which provide the enormous subsidies propping up modern intensive farming, and thirdly to clean up the mess that modern farming leaves behind.

So can the true cost of food be brought down? Breaking away from industrial agriculture as the solution to hunger may be very hard for some countries, but in Britain, where the immediate need to supply food is less urgent, and the costs and the damage of intensive farming have been clearly seen, it may be more feasible. The government needs to create sustainable, competitive and diverse farming and food sectors, which will contribute to a thriving and sustainable rural economy, and advance environmental, economic, health, and animal welfare goals.

But if industrial agriculture is to be replaced, what is a viable alternative? Professor Pretty feels that organic farming would be too big a jump in thinking and in practices for many farmers. Furthermore, the price premium would put the produce out of reach of many poorer consumers. He is recommending the immediate introduction of a ‘Greener Food Standard’, which would push the market towards more sustainable environmental practices than the current norm, while not requiring the full commitment to organic production. Such a standard would comprise agreed practices for different kinds of farming, covering agrochemical use, soil health, land management, water and energy use, food safety and animal health. It could go a long way, he says, to shifting consumers as well as farmers towards a more sustainable system of agriculture.

answerEvidence.evidence: £23m for the removal of the bug cryptosporidium from drinking water by water companies
answerEvidence.reason: Removing a contaminating organism from drinking water is a domestic-water purification cost.

distractors.A: Paragraph A mentions water pollution only as general collateral damage and gives no purification cost.
distractors.B: Paragraph B describes ecological damage and fertiliser run-off, not the cost of purifying domestic water.
distractors.C: Paragraph C explains the concept of externalities, not a water-treatment expense.
distractors.D: Paragraph D gives an aggregate estimate of agricultural externalities, not the specific domestic-water purification item.
distractors.F: Paragraph F proposes a more sustainable farming economy and contains no water-purification cost.
distractors.G: Paragraph G proposes a Greener Food Standard and contains no water-purification cost.

answerEvidence.evidence: First mechanisation, then mass use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, then monocultures, then battery rearing of livestock, and now genetic engineering — the onward march of intensive farming has seemed unstoppable in the last half-century, as the yields of produce have soared.
answerEvidence.reason: The repeated sequence first/then/then/then/now explicitly traces successive stages in farming development.

distractors.A: Paragraph A contrasts cheap food with its collateral damage but does not set out the industry’s successive stages.
distractors.C: Paragraph C defines hidden external costs rather than narrating the development of farming methods.
distractors.D: Paragraph D quantifies external costs for one year rather than describing historical stages.
distractors.E: Paragraph E itemises costs and three forms of payment, not stages in farming development.
distractors.F: Paragraph F discusses moving away from intensive agriculture, not how that industry developed.
distractors.G: Paragraph G presents possible alternatives and standards, not the historical stages of the industry.

answerEvidence.evidence: That is mainly because the costs of all this damage are what economists refer to as externalities: they are outside the main transaction
answerEvidence.reason: The paragraph explicitly names hidden costs outside the main transaction as externalities.

distractors.A: Paragraph A calls the harm collateral damage but does not supply the economists’ term requested.
distractors.B: Paragraph B lists environmental damage without naming the hidden-cost concept.
distractors.D: Paragraph D calculates the costs but does not introduce the requested term.
distractors.E: Paragraph E itemises external costs and payment routes but does not define the term.
distractors.F: Paragraph F considers reducing intensive farming and contains no hidden-cost terminology.
distractors.G: Paragraph G considers alternatives and standards and contains no hidden-cost terminology.

answerEvidence.evidence: Natural soil fertility is dropping in many areas because of continuous industrial fertiliser and pesticide use, while the growth of algae is increasing in lakes because of the fertiliser run-off.
answerEvidence.reason: The sentence states a concrete effect of agricultural chemicals on a water source: fertiliser run-off increases algae in lakes.

distractors.A: Paragraph A mentions water pollution in a general list but does not identify a specific chemical effect on a water source.
distractors.C: Paragraph C explains why consumers do not see external costs and gives no chemical effect on water.
distractors.D: Paragraph D quantifies aggregate damage and gives no chemical effect on water sources.
distractors.E: Paragraph E lists removal costs for pollutants but not an ecological effect caused by chemicals in a water source.
distractors.F: Paragraph F proposes policy change and gives no chemical effect on water.
distractors.G: Paragraph G outlines a farming standard and gives no chemical effect on water.

answerEvidence.evidence: In Britain, for example, many of our best-loved farmland birds, such as the skylark, the grey partridge, the lapwing and the corn bunting, have vanished from huge stretches of countryside, as have even more wild flowers and insects.
answerEvidence.reason: The explicit disappearance of numerous bird, flower and insect species supports the claim of wildlife decline.

distractors.NO: NO would contradict the explicit report that many species have vanished from large areas.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: NOT GIVEN is impossible because the passage directly describes the decline of several kinds of British wildlife.

answerEvidence.evidence: The passage contains no statement comparing the taste of food in recent years with its taste in the past.
answerEvidence.reason: Food price, production damage, health and policy are discussed, but no change in taste is stated.

distractors.YES: YES would require an explicit claim that food tastes worse now; the passage makes no such claim.
distractors.NO: NO would require an explicit claim that taste has stayed the same or improved; the passage makes no such claim.

answerEvidence.evidence: To many, the costs may not even appear to be financial at all, but merely aesthetic – a terrible shame, but nothing to do with money.
answerEvidence.reason: The writer says many people do not even recognise the damage as financial, directly contradicting widely recognised.

distractors.YES: YES reverses the writer’s explicit point that consumers rarely make the connection.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: NOT GIVEN is wrong because the passage directly addresses whether people recognise these financial costs.

answerEvidence.reason: Food poisoning is illness caused by food and is explicitly included among Professor Pretty’s calculated costs.

distractors.NO: NO contradicts the explicit £169m cost assigned to food poisoning.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: NOT GIVEN is wrong because food poisoning appears directly in the itemised calculation.

answerEvidence.evidence: Professor Pretty draws a simple but memorable conclusion from all this: our food bills are actually threefold.
answerEvidence.reason: Threefold food bills/costs are higher than the single visible shop payment most people perceive.

answerEvidence.evidence: Breaking away from industrial agriculture as the solution to hunger may be very hard for some countries, but in Britain, where the immediate need to supply food is less urgent, and the costs and the damage of intensive farming have been clearly seen, it may be more feasible.
answerEvidence.reason: For Britain, breaking away from intensive farming is presented as feasible; the official key permits modern as an optional modifier.

answerEvidence.evidence: Professor Pretty feels that organic farming would be too big a jump in thinking and in practices for many farmers.
answerEvidence.reason: Too big a jump paraphrases the summary’s statement that most farmers would be unable to adapt to it.

answerEvidence.evidence: He is recommending the immediate introduction of a ‘Greener Food Standard’, which would push the market towards more sustainable environmental practices than the current norm, while not requiring the full commitment to organic production.
answerEvidence.reason: This is the named standard Professor Pretty recommends the government introduce.

answerEvidence.evidence: It could go a long way, he says, to shifting consumers as well as farmers towards a more sustainable system of agriculture.
answerEvidence.reason: The proposed standard is intended to shift both groups; the official key accepts farmers and consumers in either order.

It has now reached a point where a growing number of people believe that it is far too high, and that bringing it down will be one of the great challenges of the twenty first century. That cost, however, is not in immediate cash. In the West at least, most food is now far cheaper to buy in relative terms than it was in 1960. The cost is in the collateral damage of the very methods of food production that have made the food cheaper: in the pollution of water, the enervation of soil, the destruction of wildlife, the harm to animal welfare and the threat to human health caused by modern industrial agriculture.
B
First mechanisation, then mass use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, then monocultures, then battery rearing of livestock, and now genetic engineering — the onward march of intensive farming has seemed unstoppable in the last half-century, as the yields of produce have soared. But the damage it has caused has been colossal. In Britain, for example, many of our best-loved farmland birds, such as the skylark, the grey partridge, the lapwing and the corn bunting, have vanished from huge stretches of countryside, as have even more wild flowers and insects. This is a direct result of the way we have produced our food in the last four decades. Thousands of miles of hedgerows, thousands of ponds, have disappeared from the landscape. The faecal filth of salmon farming has driven wild salmon from many of the sea lochs and rivers of Scotland. Natural soil fertility is dropping in many areas because of continuous industrial fertiliser and pesticide use, while the growth of algae is increasing in lakes because of the fertiliser run-off.
C
Put it all together and it looks like a battlefield, but consumers rarely make the connection at the dinner table. That is mainly because the costs of all this damage are what economists refer to as externalities: they are outside the main transaction, which is for example producing and selling a field of wheat, and are borne directly by neither producers nor consumers. To many, the costs may not even appear to be financial at all, but merely aesthetic – a terrible shame, but nothing to do with money. And anyway they, as consumers of food, certainly aren’t paying for it, are they?
pages.49:
D
But the costs to society can actually be quantified and, when added up, can amount to staggering sums. A remarkable exercise in doing this has been carried out by one of the world’s leading thinkers on the future of agriculture, Professor Jules Pretty, Director of the Centre for Environment and Society at the University of Essex. Professor Pretty and his colleagues calculated the externalities of British agriculture for one particular year. They added up the costs of repairing the damage it caused, and came up with a total figure of £2,343m. This is equivalent to £208 for every hectare of arable land and permanent pasture, almost as much again as the total government and EU spend on British farming in that year. And according to Professor Pretty, it was a conservative estimate.
E
The costs included: £120m for removal of pesticides; £16m for removal of nitrates; £55m for removal of phosphates and soil; £23m for the removal of the bug cryptosporidium from drinking water by water companies; £125m for damage to wildlife habitats, hedgerows and dry stone walls; £1,113m from emissions of gases likely to contribute to climate change; £106m from soil erosion and organic carbon losses; £169m from food poisoning; and £607m from cattle disease. Professor Pretty draws a simple but memorable conclusion from all this: our food bills are actually threefold. We are paying for our supposedly cheaper food in three separate ways: once over the counter, secondly through our taxes, which provide the enormous subsidies propping up modern intensive farming, and thirdly to clean up the mess that modern farming leaves behind.
F
So can the true cost of food be brought down? Breaking away from industrial agriculture as the solution to hunger may be very hard for some countries, but in Britain, where the immediate need to supply food is less urgent, and the costs and the damage of intensive farming have been clearly seen, it may be more feasible. The government needs to create sustainable, competitive and diverse farming and food sectors, which will contribute to a thriving and sustainable rural economy, and advance environmental, economic, health, and animal welfare goals.
G
But if industrial agriculture is to be replaced, what is a viable alternative? Professor Pretty feels that organic farming would be too big a jump in thinking and in practices for many farmers. Furthermore, the price premium would put the produce out of reach of many poorer consumers. He is recommending the immediate introduction of a ‘Greener Food Standard’, which would push the market towards more sustainable environmental practices than the current norm, while not requiring the full commitment to organic production. Such a standard would comprise agreed practices for different kinds of farming, covering agrochemical use, soil health, land management, water and energy use, food safety and animal health. It could go a long way, he says, to shifting consumers as well as farmers towards a more sustainable system of agriculture.
